title: Dwarf Irregular Galaxy UGC 8091
caption: Dwarf irregular galaxy UGC 8091, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGC 8091 · constellation Virgo · about 7.9 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble, NASA, ESA, Yumi Choi (NSF's NOIRLab), Karoline Gilbert (STScI), Julianne Dalcanton (Center for Computational Astrophysics/Flatiron Inst., UWashington)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A dense spread of blue and orange stars fills most of the frame, with patches of blue toward the middle and distant galaxies scattered across the dark background. This is UGC 8091, a dwarf galaxy of about a billion stars, approximately 7 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. NASA likens it to a sparkling snow globe.

UGC 8091 counts as an irregular galaxy because it has no orderly spiral or elliptical shape, and its stars look more like a tangle of string lights. Some irregular galaxies may have been scrambled by violent activity inside them, while others took shape through encounters with neighboring galaxies, so the class comes in many sizes and forms.

The red patches are likely hydrogen gas glowing because light from hot, energetic stars has excited it. The other sparkles are a mix of older stars. The observing programs behind the image looked at the part dwarf galaxies played, billions of years ago, in heating up again the hydrogen that cooled as the young universe expanded.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's WFC3 and ACS cameras. NASA shows F218N, F225W and F275W in purple, F336W, F373N and F487N in blue, F475W and F502N in cyan, F475W in green, F814W in orange, and F656N, F657N, F110W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Part of the light is ultraviolet, which the eye cannot see, and the picture combines exposures gathered over many years.

explore: Twelve filters were combined for the image, covering light from the mid-ultraviolet to the red end of the visible spectrum. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys gathered the data between 2006 and 2021. Astronomers are also studying what dwarf galaxies and their stars are made of, to trace links between such ancient galaxies and modern ones like the Milky Way.
